parts: Lesson 12: Long-term Sources of Business Finance — Summary

Funds not to be paid back within one year are long-term finance (also called fixed capital). Need: to buy fixed assets (land, building, plant, machinery), for restructuring (mergers, acquisitions, takeovers, modernisation), research and development, marketing strategy and the non-fluctuating (permanent) part of working capital. Sources may be internal (retained earnings) or external (shares, debentures, loans, public deposits, lease) and domestic or foreign.

The part of profit not distributed but reinvested is retained earnings or ploughing back of profits (kept in General Reserve, Debenture Redemption Reserve, Dividend Equalisation Reserve). Merits: cheap source (no issue expenses, no obligation to pay interest or repay); financial stability; benefits to shareholders (stable dividend, bonus shares, capital appreciation). Demerits: possible only with high profits for many years; may dissatisfy shareholders expecting dividends; may result in mismanagement of funds.

A share is the smallest unit of the company's capital. Equity shares carry no preferential right; the dividend is paid after preference shares at a fluctuating rate depending on profit; in winding up the capital is repaid last; holders are owners with voting rights (ownership capital). Merits: owners' say, liability limited to face value, no obligation on the company to pay dividend or repay in lifetime, no charge on assets. Demerits: dividend only if profits, speculation, high risk, procedural delay and higher cost, control may be grabbed by groups. Issue is through stock markets (NSE, BSE) or private placement (angel investors, venture capitalists, private equity).

Preference shares carry preferential rights for dividend (fixed rate) and return of capital; no voting rights. Types: convertible and non-convertible; cumulative (arrears carried forward) and non-cumulative; participating and non-participating; redeemable (fixed maturity) and irredeemable (repaid only on liquidation).

A debenture is a written acknowledgement of money borrowed (debt capital) with a fixed rate of interest; holders are creditors, get interest irrespective of profit and have no voting rights. Merits: secured; assured return; trading on equity; no dilution of control; interest is a tax-deductible expense. Demerits: fixed obligation to pay interest and principal; creates a charge on assets; reduces borrowing capacity. Types: redeemable and irredeemable (perpetual); convertible and non-convertible; secured (mortgaged) and unsecured (naked); registered and bearer (transferable by delivery; company keeps no record).

Shares versus debentures: shareholders are owners, debenture holders are creditors; dividend varies with profit while interest is fixed; shareholders vote and debenture holders do not; shares need no security while debentures are generally secured; shares are repaid after debentures; shares are riskier.

Loans from special financial institutions (IFCI, SFCs, SIDCs): up to 25 years, large amounts, lower rates but long formalities; they may nominate directors. Commercial bank term loans: 3 to 5 years, flexible, secrecy, lower cost and time, no interference; need security and many formalities. Public deposits: invited from shareholders, employees and the public for 6 to 60 months; simple, no charge on assets, economical, flexible; but uncertain, insecure and limited in amount. Lease financing: the lessor owns the asset and the lessee uses it on rent; sale and lease back is the sale of an existing asset to a lessor and leasing it back. Merits: lower investment, simple documentation, tax-deductible rentals, no dilution of control, no effect on debt capacity, obsolescence risk with the lessor. Demerits: restrictions on use, effects if the lease is not renewed, higher payout on premature termination, no ownership or residual value.

American Depository Receipts (ADRs) are issued by a US bank for trading only in American markets. Global Depository Receipts (GDRs): shares converted into dollar-denominated receipts by an international bank and sold globally; holders get dividend but no voting rights. Loans from multinational financial institutions (World Bank, IFC). External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs): foreign currency borrowings with lower rates but currency risk. Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs): equity-linked debt convertible into equity or depository receipts. Non-Resident Indian (NRI) financing: sale of shares to NRIs within prescribed limits.

Factors: cost (of procurement and of utilisation); financial strength and stability of operations; form of organisation and legal status (a partnership cannot issue shares); purpose and time period; risk profile; control; effect on credit-worthiness; flexibility and ease; tax benefits.
